---
title: "Doing the work"
description: "What each assurance level requires, phase by phase, and what to record as you go."
---

*Phases 1 to 4, the whole of producing the analysis. [Where this sits in the lifecycle](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd).*

You have a level from [section 5](../05-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd). This section says
what to do about it.

**Read the column for your level. You do not need the other two.**

**Level 4 BCA is not a fourth column here.** Its checks are additional to Level 3's, and
everything that is true only of Business Critical work is in
[section 8](../08-business-critical/index.qmd). If you scored 4 on any impact dimension, read
the Level 3 column here and then go there.

## Your level in one line

### Level 1 Standard

Produce the analysis well and record enough that someone could re-run it. One colleague checks your
headline numbers. No separate assurance plan. A quality assurance statement is optional.

### Level 2 Enhanced

Everything above, plus **someone who had no hand in the work reviews it**. You name that reviewer
before you start, you log the checks as you do them, and you produce a quality assurance statement.
Your team lead signs it off.

### Level 3 Comprehensive

Everything above, plus **an assurer from outside your team**, full verification and validation, code
assured, uncertainty quantified where the method allows, and the statement published with the
output. Signed off by Head of Profession or Analysis Senior Responsible Officer.

Each step up buys one specific thing: Level 2 buys separation from the work, Level 3 buys separation
from the team plus published transparency. They differ in kind, not just in volume.

## The procedure, phase by phase

Phases follow [section 4, the analytical lifecycle](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd).

### Phase 1: engagement and scoping

| | Level 1 Standard | Level 2 Enhanced | Level 3 Comprehensive |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Commission and frame** | Commissioner states the decision and the deadline. You confirm your understanding in writing, however briefly. An email is enough | The commissioning conversation is recorded: the decision, the question, what is out of scope, and the quality expected | Formal commissioning record. Analysis Senior Responsible Officer or Head of Service aware. Business Critical status considered explicitly and recorded either way |
| **Set the level** | You score it and record it in your project record | You and the commissioner agree it together. Disagreement goes to the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead | The Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead confirms it. Register entry where Business Critical |

At every level you may reframe a request that arrives as an output rather than a question.
Providing appropriate challenge is expected of you.[^src-govs-010-section-6-2]

The level belongs here rather than at design because the specification agreed with your commissioner
is where the required level of assurance is defined.[^src-aqua-book-section-6-1-2] Design is where you
plan how to deliver it.

### Phase 2: design

| | Level 1 Standard | Level 2 Enhanced | Level 3 Comprehensive |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plan the assurance** | Note your method and main assumptions. No separate assurance plan | An assurance plan: who reviews, what, and when. **The reviewer is named before work starts** | Assurance plan agreed with an assurer from outside your team. Verification and validation activities specified |
| **Book the time** | Allow for the colleague check | Assurer's time in the schedule, agreed with them | Assurer's time agreed and protected. Re-review time allowed for[^src-aqua-book-section-7-1-3] |
| **Design gate** | Not required | A critical friend confirms the approach answers the question and the assurance planned is right. Commissioner approves the design before work proceeds[^src-govs-010-section-5-3] | As Level 2, with the assurer from outside the team |

Naming your reviewer before you start is what makes Level 2 different from Level 1. A reviewer found
afterwards reviews what was produced. A reviewer named beforehand shapes what gets produced.

::: {.callout-note title="Finding a critical friend" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Assign one early, ideally while you are still defining the problem. Contact the Data Science team or
the Data Science Lead if you need a recommendation. This is the role
[section 3](../03-roles-and-responsibilities/index.qmd) calls the critical friend, or analytical
assurer.

Choose someone with experience of similar data or techniques. If you are the area expert, consider a
newer colleague instead: they gain the experience, and you get genuinely fresh eyes.

Involve them throughout rather than at the end. Meet regularly, review in small increments, plan
their time into your schedule, and give notice when you need a review.
:::

### Phase 3: analysis

| | Level 1 Standard | Level 2 Enhanced | Level 3 Comprehensive |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Produce** | Keep inputs and working reproducible enough that someone else could re-run it | Work under version control. Log decisions and assumption changes as they happen | Maintain an assumptions register. Plan sensitivity testing at design stage, not afterwards |
| **Quality assure** | Self-check against the Level 1 checks. A colleague sanity-checks your headline numbers | **Independent peer review by someone outside the work.** Code review where scripted. Quality assurance log completed and retained | Full verification and validation. Code assured. Uncertainty documented and quantified where the method allows |

Where your analysis involves code, follow the
[NHSBSA Analytical Code Assurance Playbook](https://nhsbsa-data-analytics.github.io/nhsbsa-analytical-code-assurance-playbook)
for version control, testing, peer review and documentation.

#### Reproducible and automated are not the same thing

**Repeatable** is the first letter of RIGOUR, and it is the one most often taken to mean
"automated". While both reproducible and automated analysis aim for efficiency and reliability,
they focus on different aspects of the process. Automation *can* contribute to reproducibility, but
automation alone is not enough.

- **Reproducibility.** Can someone else, or even you later on, given the *same* inputs,
  *understand* and *recreate* your work?
- **Automation.** Can a computer *run* the analysis, with *any* valid inputs, with minimal or no
  human intervention?

Best practice is a fully reproducible analysis that includes a level of automation appropriate to
the complexity and the effort of repeating it manually.

| Consideration | Reproducible analysis | Automated analysis |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary goal** | Verifiability, transparency, reusability | Efficiency, scalability, speed |
| **Main activities** | Documenting all steps and key decisions, managing versions | Scripting, scheduling, pipelines, monitoring |
| **Does it require automation?** | No | Yes |
| **Is it essential?** | Yes | No, but desirable, especially as an analysis grows in complexity |
| **Testing the analysis** | Use static input data, for known results | Include tests that run automatically when the analysis changes |
| **Consistency** | In results | In processes |

Three places go further:
[Quality Assurance of Code for Analysis and Research](https://best-practice-and-impact.github.io/qa-of-code-guidance/principles.html#reproducible)
for the principle itself,
[What is RAP?](https://nhsdigital.github.io/rap-community-of-practice/introduction_to_RAP/what_is_RAP/#automation)
for the automation half, and the
[NHSBSA Analytical Code Assurance Playbook](https://nhsbsa-data-analytics.github.io/nhsbsa-analytical-code-assurance-playbook)
for testing analytical pipelines, documentation and a modular approach.

### Phase 4: delivery and sign-off

| | Level 1 Standard | Level 2 Enhanced | Level 3 Comprehensive |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Communicate** | State your main limitation alongside the result. Quality assurance statement optional | Quality assurance statement required. Caveats, limitations and uncertainty stated **in the output itself, not only in an annex** | Statement published with the output. Uncertainty ranges communicated. Algorithm Transparency Recording Standard entry where an algorithmic tool is involved |
| **Sign off and archive** | Store the project record with the output. No formal sign-off beyond you | **Signed off by your team lead.** Project record, quality assurance log and code archived together and linked from the output | Signed off by Head of Profession or Analysis Senior Responsible Officer. Register updated. Review date set |

Delivered results include an assurance statement covering assumptions, uncertainty, limitations and
what the results can and cannot be used for. GovS 010 section 5.5 puts this as a should; here it is
a condition of sign-off at every level.
[Section 9, communicating analysis](../09-communicating-analysis/index.qmd), shows what that looks
like written out.

## What to record

Keep records proportionate.[^src-govs-010-section-6-7] The project record is one place for everything
about a piece of analysis, and how much of it you complete depends on your level.

| Section of the project record | Level 1 | Level 2 | Level 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Header: title, reference, level, analyst, commissioner, dates, Business Critical yes or no | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| 2. The question: the decision it supports, the question, what is out of scope, the deadline | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| 3. Data: source, owner, extract date, known quality issues, effect on the analysis, access basis | Not required | Yes | Yes |
| 4. Method: approach, why this and not the alternatives, tools and code repository | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| 5. Assumptions: assumption, rationale, impact if wrong, sensitivity tested, agreed with | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| 6. Uncertainty: principal sources, how quantified or why not, how communicated | Not required | Yes | Yes, quantified |
| 7. Decision log, including **deviations from the plan** | Not required | Yes | Yes |
| 8. Assurance and sign-off: role, name, date, what they confirmed | Not required | Yes | Yes, plus approver |
| 9. **Lessons learned** | Not required | Yes | Yes |

::: {.callout-important title="Level 1 is one side of A4" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Level 1 completes sections 1, 2, 4 and 5 only. That is realistically one side of A4.

A record that demands twelve pages for two hours of analysis will not get completed, and a record
nobody completes is worse than none, because it looks like assurance from a distance.
:::

Identify relevant lessons from earlier work when you plan, and capture new ones as you go rather
than reconstructing them at the end.[^src-govs-010-sections-6-7-and-6-10]

Records should be version controlled, securely stored and retrievable.[^src-govs-010-section-6-7]

## The checks, by level

**These are NHSBSA's own checks, from the decision sheet.** They are cumulative: each level does
everything the levels below it do, and adds what is in its own block. Your quality assurance log
records which you did, when, and what you found.

{{< include /guidance/_partials/diagram-levels.qmd >}}

| First required at | Check | What that means here |
|---|---|---|
| **Level 1** | Validation of requirements | The question, the decision it informs and what is out of scope are confirmed in writing with the commissioner |
| **Level 1** | Specification, user guide and notes | Enough written down that someone else could pick the work up. At this level it is short |
| **Level 1** | Data sources and assumptions clear | Source, extract date and provenance recorded. Assumptions listed with the rationale and the effect if wrong. Known data quality issues named, with their effect stated |
| **Level 1** | Accuracy of data transformations and calculations | You check your own transformations and totals. A colleague sanity-checks the headline numbers |
| **Level 1** | Methodological correctness | The method is documented, with the alternatives you considered and why you did not use them |
| **Level 1** | Sense checking results | Outputs compared against an independent reference: last period, a related series, or an order-of-magnitude expectation |
| **Level 1** | Clarity, accessibility and security of outputs | Limitations stated in the output itself rather than only in an annex. Accessible format. Handled at the right classification |
| **Level 2** | Responsibilities and accountabilities | The analyst, the reviewer and the approver are named before the work starts, not found afterwards |
| **Level 2** | Appropriateness of methodology | Someone who had no hand in the work agrees the method answers the question |
| **Level 2** | Documentation and audit trails | The quality assurance log is completed as you go and retained with the analysis |
| **Level 2** | Understanding of the impacts of data quality | Input data profiled: ranges, nulls, duplicates, outliers, and what each means for the answer |
| **Level 2** | Evidence based assumptions | Each assumption is traceable to a source, a precedent or a stated expert judgement |
| **Level 2** | Code scrutiny | Code peer reviewed and version controlled |
| **Level 2** | Validation with stakeholders and subject matter experts | The people who know the business area see the results before release and say whether they are plausible |
| **Level 2** | Sensitivity testing | Key assumptions varied to see whether the conclusion moves. Where material at this level |
| **Level 2** | Triangulation and independent validation of results | Calculations independently reproduced from source by the reviewer |
| **Level 3** | Change control processes | Changes to data, method or code after sign-off are recorded and re-assured proportionately |
| **Level 3** | Ethical risks | Assessed against the Data and AI Ethics Framework, per [section 10](../10-ethics-and-transparency/index.qmd) |
| **Level 3** | Knowledge sharing | The method and the lessons are shared beyond the delivering team |
| **Level 3** | Detailed documentation review | The assurer reads the documentation as a document, not only the numbers |
| **Level 3** | Usability testing | The output is tested with someone who will use it, not only with someone who made it |
| **Level 3** | Automated checks | Validation built into the pipeline so it runs every time rather than once |
| **Level 3** | Additional scenario testing | Behaviour under plausible alternative inputs, not just the expected ones |
| **Level 3** | Independent peer review | An assurer from outside the delivering team. Code assured against the [NHSBSA Analytical Code Assurance Playbook](https://nhsbsa-data-analytics.github.io/nhsbsa-analytical-code-assurance-playbook). Uncertainty quantified where the method allows. Quality assurance statement published with the output |
| **Level 4 BCA** | Formal audits | See [section 8](../08-business-critical/index.qmd) |
| **Level 4 BCA** | External review | As above |
| **Level 4 BCA** | Additional scrutiny of documentation | As above |
| **Level 4 BCA** | Scrutiny of structural and conceptual assumptions | As above |
| **Level 4 BCA** | Additional scenario testing | As above |

The Level 4 row is deliberately thin here. Everything that is true only of Business Critical work,
including the register entry, the QA appraisal and the documentation stack, is in
[section 8](../08-business-critical/index.qmd).

An Algorithm Transparency Recording Standard entry is completed where an algorithmic tool informs a
decision affecting the public, from Level 3 upwards. See
[section 10](../10-ethics-and-transparency/index.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Why the log matters more than the checklist" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
A checklist shows somebody knew what to do. A log shows they did it, when, and what they found.
GovS 010 requires you to document verification and validation activities **and the conclusions you
drew from them**, so that the reliability of the analysis can be assessed afterwards.[^src-govs-010-section-6-6]

Keep the log with the analysis wherever you can. A log stored somewhere else is a log that does not
get filled in.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Peer review here, the Review stage in section 11" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
The peer review and independent challenge on this page happen **during** the work. They check that
the question is answered, that the method was appropriate, that the checks were at the right level
and that the audit trail holds, and they gate release. That is GovS 010 sections 6.6 and 6.8.

**A different thing is also called review.** What happens to an output after it is released, whether
it is still useful, and what the next piece of work should do differently, is
[section 11](../11-review-and-continuous-improvement/index.qmd). That is GovS 010 sections 6.10 and
6.13.

If you are here looking for the monthly review of regular outputs, section 11 is the page you want.
:::
